items.stem:
(i) Define a decomposition reaction. Write chemical equation for the reaction that occurs when lead nitrate is heated strongly in a boiling tube.
(ii) In electrolytic decomposition of water two gases are liberated at the electrodes. Give the mass ratio of the gas liberated at the cathode and at the anode.
items.answer:
(i) The reactions in which a single reactant breaks down to form two or more substances in the presence of heat, light or electricity are known as decomposition reactions.
(ii) 2Pb(NO₃)₂(s) —Heat→ 2PbO(s) [lead oxide, yellow] + 4NO₂(g) [brown] + O₂(g)
2H₂O(l) —Electricity→ 2H₂(g) [at cathode] + O₂(g) [at anode]
Mass of H₂ evolved at cathode = 2 × 2 = 4 g
Mass of O₂ evolved at anode = 1 × 32 = 32 g
Mass of H₂ : Mass of O₂ = 4 : 32 = 1 : 8
items.ocr: The worked solution was one collapsed LaTeX array: 'Read oride' (lead oxide), 'ANO_2' (4NO₂), 'Xelow' (brown) and the electrolysis line were unreadable. Both equations restored with their arrows and coefficients from the stated 1:8 mass ratio and standard lead nitrate decomposition.

items.stem:
Identify the type of each of the following reactions stating reason for your answers:
(a) Fe₂O₃ + 2Al → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe + heat
(b) Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2KI → PbI₂ + 2KNO₃
(c) ZnCO₃ —heat→ ZnO + CO₂
items.answer:
(a) Single displacement reaction. Aluminium (Al), being more reactive than iron (Fe), displaces the less reactive metal Fe from its compound Fe₂O₃. This displacement is highly exothermic and releases a lot of heat.
(b) Double displacement reaction. The two compounds Pb(NO₃)₂ and KI react by exchange of ions to form two new compounds, lead iodide and potassium nitrate: Pb²⁺ of Pb(NO₃)₂ combines with 2I⁻ of 2KI to form PbI₂, and 2K⁺ of 2KI combines with 2NO₃⁻ of Pb(NO₃)₂ to form 2KNO₃. Since PbI₂ is formed as a precipitate (an insoluble solid) which separates out from the solution, this reaction is also a precipitation reaction.
(c) Thermal decomposition reaction. A single compound, zinc carbonate (ZnCO₃), on heating breaks down into two compounds, zinc oxide (ZnO) and carbon dioxide (CO₂). When a decomposition reaction is carried out by heating, it is called a thermal decomposition reaction.
items.ocr: The three equations were printed as a single LaTeX array with the labels '(b) (c)' dumped afterwards; labels re-attached to their equations. 'Kl' read as KI and 'Pbl_2' as PbI₂ throughout; 'Fe O ~3~' read as Fe₂O₃.

items.stem:
When hydrogen sulphide gas is passed through a blue solution of copper sulphate, the colour of the solution fades and a black precipitate is obtained.
(a) Name the type of reaction mentioned above.
(b) Why does the colour of the solution fade away?
(c) Write the chemical name of the black precipitate formed.
(d) Give the balanced chemical equation for the reaction involved.
items.answer:
When hydrogen sulphide gas is passed through a blue solution of copper sulphate, the blue colour of the solution fades and a black precipitate of copper sulphide is formed along with sulphuric acid.
(a) The reaction is a double displacement reaction.
(b) The blue colour of copper sulphate fades because it reacts with hydrogen sulphide gas, giving a colourless solution of sulphuric acid.
(c) The chemical name of the black precipitate is copper sulphide.
(d) H₂S(g) + CuSO₄(aq) → CuS(s) + H₂SO₄(aq)
   hydrogen sulphide gas + copper sulphate solution (blue) → copper sulphide (black) + sulphuric acid
items.ocr: The equation printed as 'H S g) + CuSO 4 aq) CuS s) .+ H SO 4 aq)' — subscripts, brackets and the reaction arrow all lost; restored as H₂S(g) + CuSO₄(aq) → CuS(s) + H₂SO₄(aq). 'balck' read as 'black'.

items.stem:
Study the figure given below and answer the following questions:
(a) Name the process depicted in the diagram.
(b) Write the composition of the anode and the cathode.
(c) Write the balanced chemical equation of the reaction taking place in this case.
(d) The reaction does not take place if a few drops of dilute sulphuric acid are not added to water. Why?
items.answer:
(a) Electrolytic decomposition of water / electrolysis of water.
(b) The gas collected at the cathode is hydrogen and its volume is double that of the gas at the anode. The gas collected at the anode is oxygen, whose volume is half that of hydrogen.
(c) 2H₂O(l) —Electric current→ 2H₂(g) + O₂(g)
(d) Water is not a good conductor of electricity, so a few drops of sulphuric acid are added to the water to make it a good conductor. Without the acid the reaction does not take place.
items.ocr: Two sentences about iodine/thyroxine causing goitre and insulin deficiency causing diabetes bled into this worked solution from a different chapter's page and have been removed. Reaction arrow in (c) restored from the LaTeX.

items.stem:
In the electrolysis of water:
(a) Name the gases liberated at anode and cathode.
(b) Why is it that the volume of gas collected on one electrode is two times that on the other electrode? What would happen if dil. H₂SO₄ is not added to water?
items.answer:
(a) Gas liberated at the anode is oxygen and the gas liberated at the cathode is hydrogen.
(b) On electrolysis water decomposes into hydrogen and oxygen:
2H₂O(l) —Electric current→ 2H₂(g) + O₂(g)
Water decomposes into hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 2 : 1 by volume, so the gas collected in double volume is hydrogen.
If dilute sulphuric acid is not added to water, electrolysis will not take place, because distilled water is not a good conductor and with tap water the conductivity is very low. Sulphuric acid is added to water to make it a good conductor.

items.stem:
Lead nitrate solution is added to a test tube containing potassium iodide solution.
(a) Write the name and colour of the compound precipitated.
(b) Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction involved.
(c) Name the type of this reaction justifying your answer.
items.answer:
(a) When lead nitrate solution is added to a test tube containing potassium iodide solution, a yellow precipitate of lead iodide is produced along with potassium nitrate solution.
(b) Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2KI(aq) → PbI₂(s) (yellow ppt.) + 2KNO₃(aq)
(c) The reaction is a double displacement reaction. Two compounds, lead nitrate solution and potassium iodide solution, react to form two new compounds, lead iodide and potassium nitrate, by an exchange of ions. The lead ions (Pb²⁺) of lead nitrate react with the iodide ions (I⁻) of potassium iodide to form the new compound lead iodide (PbI₂), and the potassium ions (K⁺) of potassium iodide react with the nitrate ions (NO₃⁻) of lead nitrate to form the new compound potassium nitrate (KNO₃). Since lead iodide (PbI₂) is formed as an insoluble yellow precipitate, it is also called a precipitation reaction.

items.stem: 1 g of copper powder was taken in a china dish and heated. What change takes place on heating? When hydrogen gas is passed over this heated substance, a visible change is seen in it. Give the chemical equations of the reactions, and the name and the colour of the products formed in each case.
items.answer:
When 1 g of copper powder is heated in a china dish, a black coating of copper(II) oxide (cupric oxide) is formed on the surface of the copper.
2Cu(s) + O₂(g) —Heat→ 2CuO(s)
The product is copper(II) oxide and it is black in colour.
When hydrogen gas is passed over copper(II) oxide, CuO is reduced to copper.
CuO(s) + H₂(g) —Heat→ Cu(s) + H₂O(l)
The product formed is Cu and its colour is reddish brown.
Explanation: In the first reaction copper has been oxidised to CuO. Since oxygen is added, it is an oxidation reaction and oxygen is the oxidising agent. In the second reaction CuO has reacted with H₂ and oxygen has been removed, so it is a reduction reaction and hydrogen is the reducing agent.
items.ocr: 'on the surface of copper of copper (ii) oxide' had a duplicated phrase, removed. The explanation block printed the equation unbalanced as 'Cu + O₂ → 2CuO' with a stray 'Oxidation'/'Reduction' caption floating free; balanced to 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO and the captions folded into the prose.

items.stem: What does a balanced chemical equation convey?
items.answer:
A balanced chemical equation conveys the following information:
(i) Formulae of the substances taking part in the chemical reaction, i.e. the reactants.
(ii) Formulae of the substances produced in the reaction, i.e. the products.
(iii) The relative number of molecules of reactants and products.
(iv) The relative masses of reactants and products.
(v) The relative volumes of the gaseous substances involved in the reaction.

items.stem: What is a thermochemical equation? Give two examples.
items.answer:
An equation in which information about the heat change is included is called a thermochemical equation. In such an equation it is very important to indicate the physical state of the various species involved.
Examples:
C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g)   ΔH = −393.5 kJ
C(graphite) + 2H₂(g) → CH₄(g)   ΔH = +74.25 kJ
items.ocr: The two examples were printed in one LaTeX array with 'C(graphite)' broken onto its own line away from its '+2H₂(g)' continuation; rejoined. The printed sign on the methane example (ΔH = +74.25 kJ) is reproduced exactly as printed, though formation of methane is in fact exothermic.

items.stem:
Write and balance the following equations presented to you as written statements:
(i) Magnesium carbonate plus hydrochloric acid produces magnesium chloride plus water plus carbon dioxide gas.
(ii) Aluminium plus chlorine gas produces aluminium trichloride.
(iii) Nitrogen plus hydrogen produces ammonia.
items.answer:
(i) Skeletal: MgCO₃ + HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂
    Balanced: MgCO₃ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂
(ii) Skeletal: Al + Cl₂(g) → AlCl₃
    Balanced: 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃
(iii) Skeletal: N₂ + H₂ → NH₃
    Balanced: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃

items.stem:
In an experiment 20 g of zinc (A) was reacted with 20 g of iodine (B) in a 250 mL beaker containing 50 mL of water. The reaction proceeded with evolution of heat and at the end, the reaction mixture did not give any colour on adding starch solution, but some zinc was found settling at the bottom.
Zn(s) + I₂(s) → ZnI₂(s) + heat
(i) Is the reaction endothermic or exothermic?
(ii) Out of the two reactants, Zn(s) and I₂(s), which one is left unreacted? Why?
(iii) How much of (A) and (B) should be taken so that no reactant is left out at the end of the reaction?
items.answer:
(i) Exothermic.
(ii) Zinc is left unreacted, because zinc was found settling at the bottom; also no iodine is left behind, as the resulting mixture gives no colour on adding starch solution. This is because 20 g of iodine does not provide the requisite number of atoms for complete consumption of the atoms given by 20 g of zinc.
(iii) The weights of (A) and (B) should be taken so that both provide equal moles. For 65.4 g of Zn (atomic weight of Zn = 65.4), 254 g of I₂ has to be taken (atomic weight of I = 127).

items.stem: Give chemical explanation for evolution and absorption of heat in a chemical reaction.
items.answer:
Atoms in the molecule of an element or a compound are held together by chemical bonds. During a chemical reaction, bonds between the atoms of the reactants are broken and new bonds are formed between the atoms of the products. When bonds are broken, energy is absorbed, and when new bonds are formed, energy is released.
(i) If the energy released during the formation of new bonds is more than the energy used up in breaking the old bonds, the overall reaction will be exothermic (heat is evolved).
(ii) If the energy released during the formation of new bonds is less than the energy required to break the bonds, the overall reaction will be endothermic (heat is absorbed).

items.stem: Name three chemical reactions in which heat is evolved and three chemical reactions in which heat is absorbed.
items.answer:
Exothermic reactions:
(i) Oxidation of methane in the presence of air: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) + 890.0 kJ
(ii) Formation of sulphur trioxide: 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃ + 46.9 kcal
(iii) Oxidation of ammonia: 4NH₃ + 5O₂ —Pt→ 4NO + 6H₂O + 21.5 kcal
Endothermic reactions:
(i) Formation of hydrogen iodide: H₂(g) + I₂(g) → 2HI(g) − 51.9 kJ
(ii) Decomposition of calcium carbonate: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g) − 177.8 kJ
(iii) Formation of carbon disulphide: C(s) + 2S(s) → CS₂(l) − 92 kJ

items.stem: Illustrate an experiment in support of a combination reaction.
items.answer:
A piece of clean magnesium wire is held with a pair of tongs and heated over a Bunsen burner. It is seen that the wire burns with a dazzling light and forms a white powder. The white powder is magnesium oxide, which is formed by the combination of magnesium with the oxygen present in the air.
2Mg(s) + O₂(g) —combination reaction→ 2MgO(s)

items.stem: Illustrate an experiment to support a displacement reaction.
items.answer:
Some silver nitrate solution is taken in a test tube; the solution is colourless. A strip of copper is added into it. After some time it is observed that some shining crystals have been deposited on the strip and the solution becomes bluish. This is because copper replaces silver in the solution and forms a bluish copper nitrate solution, while shining crystals of silver deposit on the copper strip.
2AgNO₃ + Cu → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag

items.stem: Design an activity to show a decomposition reaction in which light is used to decompose a reactant. Write chemical equation for the reaction and state its one use.
items.answer:
Activity: Take about 2 g of silver chloride in a china dish and note down its colour. Place this china dish in sunlight for some time and observe the colour of the silver chloride after some time. The white silver chloride turns grey in sunlight. This is due to the decomposition of silver chloride into silver and chlorine by light.
2AgCl(s) —Sunlight→ 2Ag(s) + Cl₂(g)
Use: This reaction is used in black and white photography.

items.stem: Draw a labelled schematic diagram to show the electrolysis of water. Why is the amount of gas collected in one of the test tubes in this activity double the amount collected in the other?
items.answer:
A labelled diagram of the electrolysis of water is drawn showing a beaker of water with a few drops of dilute sulphuric acid, two carbon electrodes connected to a battery, and an inverted graduated test tube over each electrode.
The composition of water is H₂O, i.e. it has 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom. Therefore the ratio of the volumes of the two gases collected is 2 : 1, hydrogen (at the cathode) being double the volume of oxygen (at the anode).

items.stem:
A, B and C are three elements which undergo chemical reactions according to the following equations:
A₂O₃ + 2B → B₂O₃ + 2A
3CSO₄ + 2B → B₂(SO₄)₃ + 3C
3CO + 2A → A₂O₃ + 3C
Answer the following questions with reasons:
(a) Which element is the most reactive?
(b) Which element is the least reactive?
(c) What is the type of reactions listed above?
items.answer:
(a) B is the most reactive, as it displaces both A and C from their solutions.
(b) C is the least reactive, as it is displaced by both A and B.
(c) These are displacement reactions.

items.stem:
Take 2 g silver chloride in a china dish and place it in sunlight.
(a) Observe the colour of silver chloride after some time.
(b) What type of reaction does take place?
(c) Write the chemical reaction for the above observation.

What change will you observe if white silver chloride is placed in sunlight? Write an equation for the reaction and the type of the reaction.
items.answer:
(a) Initially silver chloride was white and after exposure to sunlight it turned grey.
(b) Decomposition reaction (photolytic decomposition).

items.stem:
Take a small amount of calcium oxide or quick lime in a beaker and slowly add water to this.
(a) Is there any change in temperature?
(b) What type of reaction is taking place?
(c) Write chemical equation for the above reaction.
items.answer:

items.answer:
X is CaCO₃ (calcium carbonate).

items.stem:
Lead nitrate solution is added to potassium iodide solution and a precipitate is formed.
(i) Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction. Name the reaction.
(ii) What is the colour of the precipitate formed and name the products formed in the reaction?
items.answer:
(i) Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2KI(aq) → PbI₂(s) + 2KNO₃(aq)

items.stem:
Account for the following:
(a) White silver chloride turns grey in sunlight.
(b) Brown coloured copper powder on heating in air turns into a black coloured substance.
items.answer:
(a) This is due to the decomposition of silver chloride into silver and chlorine in the presence of sunlight.
2AgCl —Sunlight→ 2Ag + Cl₂
(b) This is due to the oxidation of copper powder to copper oxide; copper and oxygen combine to form a new substance.
2Cu + O₂ —Heat→ 2CuO

items.stem:
Explain the following chemical changes, giving one example in each case:
(i) Displacement or substitution,
(ii) Dissociation,
(iii) Isomerisation reaction.
items.answer:
(i) Displacement or substitution reaction: The reaction in which an atom or a group of atoms in a molecule is replaced by another atom or group of atoms is called a displacement or substitution reaction. For example, zinc displaces copper from its sulphate solution.
CuSO₄ + Zn → ZnSO₄ + Cu
(ii) Dissociation reaction: When a substance breaks up into positive and negative ions in water, it is called a dissociation reaction. For example, acetic acid in water dissociates into CH₃COO⁻ and H⁺ ions.
CH₃COOH + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H₃O⁺
(iii) Isomerisation reaction: When a compound changes into another compound by simple rearrangement of atoms, it is called an isomerisation reaction. For example:
NH₄CNO —heat→ NH₂CONH₂
(ammonium cyanate → urea)

Give one example each of the following decomposition reactions. Write the balanced equation in each case.
(i) The reaction which occurs on passing electric current.
(ii) The reaction which occurs in the presence of sunlight.
(iii) The reaction which occurs on heating of a substance.
items.answer:

2H₂O —Electrolysis→ 2H₂ + O₂
(ii) Silver chloride turns grey in sunlight due to the decomposition of silver chloride into silver and chlorine by light.
2AgCl(s) —Sunlight→ 2Ag(s) + Cl₂(g)
(iii) On heating, calcium carbonate decomposes into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide. This is called thermal decomposition.
CaCO₃(s) —Heat→ CaO(s) + CO₂(g)

Take 3 g of barium hydroxide in a test tube, now add about 2 g of ammonium chloride and mix the contents with the help of a glass rod. Now touch the test tube from outside.

(ii) State the inference about the type of reaction occurred.

items.stem:
Look at the figure given below and answer the following questions:
(i) What is the colour of ferrous sulphate crystals before and after heating?
(ii) How do you identify the gases evolved on heating?
(iii) Write the balanced chemical equation. What kind of reaction does it represent?
items.answer:
(i) Before heating the crystals are green in colour; after heating they turn white (and then a brown residue of ferric oxide is left).
(ii) The gas evolved can be identified by the characteristic smell of burning sulphur.
(iii) 2FeSO₄(s) —Heat→ Fe₂O₃(s) (ferric oxide) + SO₂(g) + SO₃(g)
It represents a thermal decomposition reaction.

items.stem:
State one example each characterised by the following, along with the chemical equation:
(a) Change in state
(b) Evolution of gas
(c) Change in temperature.
items.answer:
(a) Change of water into ice is an example of a change of state.
H₂O(l) —Freeze→ H₂O(s)
(b) By placing zinc granules in H₂SO₄ solution, hydrogen gas is evolved and a zinc salt is formed. This is an example of evolution of gas.
Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂↑
(c) Calcium oxide reacts vigorously with water to produce slaked lime, releasing a large amount of heat. This is an example of change in temperature.
CaO(s) + H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq) + Heat
items.ocr: '(a) Change in stable' read as '(a) Change in state', which is what the worked solution answers. 'H_2O(1)' read as H₂O(l). No exam-paper tag is printed.

items.stem:
On heating blue coloured powder of copper(II) nitrate in a boiling tube, copper oxide (black), oxygen gas and a brown gas X is formed.
(a) Write a balanced chemical equation of the reaction.
(b) Identify the brown gas X evolved.
(c) Identify the type of reaction.
items.answer:
(a) 2Cu(NO₃)₂(s) —Heat→ 2CuO(s) + 4NO₂(g) + O₂(g)
(b) The brown gas X is nitrogen dioxide (NO₂).
(c) It is an example of a decomposition reaction (thermal decomposition).
items.ocr: The printed answer key equation is unbalanced — 'Cu(NO₃)₂(s) —Heat→ CuO(s) + 4NO₂(g) + O₂(g)' has one copper nitrate on the left but four NO₂ on the right. Balanced to 2Cu(NO₃)₂ → 2CuO + 4NO₂ + O₂.

items.stem:
Look at the figure given below and answer the following questions:
(a) Write the chemical reaction involved.
(b) What are the colours of Cu and CuO?
(c) Can we reconvert CuO into Cu? Write the reaction involved.
items.answer:
(a) 2Cu + O₂ —Heat→ 2CuO
(b) Cu powder is shiny brown while CuO is black.
(c) Yes, by heating with hydrogen gas.
CuO + H₂ —Heat→ Cu + H₂O
items.ocr: The equation in (a) printed as '2Cu + O₂ Heat 2CuO' with the arrow lost; restored.

items.stem:
Look at the figure given below and answer the following questions:
(i) Which tube contains hydrogen gas?
(ii) If the volume of hydrogen gas collected is 10 mL, what will be the volume of oxygen collected?
(iii) Why do we add a few drops of dil. sulphuric acid?
items.answer:
(i) Hydrogen gas is collected in the test tube B placed over the cathode.
(ii) The volume of O₂ gas collected will be half the volume of H₂ gas, i.e. 5 mL.
(iii) Pure water is a non-conductor of electricity. A few drops of dilute H₂SO₄ are added to conduct electricity through it.
items.ocr: In (iii) the acid printed as 'dilute SO ^4' with the H₂ lost; restored to dilute H₂SO₄.

items.stem:
During the reaction of some metals with dilute hydrochloric acid, the following observations were made:
(i) The temperature of the reaction mixture rises when aluminium (Al) is added.
(ii) The reaction of sodium metal is found to be highly explosive.
(iii) Some bubbles of a gas are seen when lead (Pb) is reacted with the acid.
Explain these observations giving suitable reasons.
items.answer:
(i) The temperature of the reaction mixture rises when aluminium is added because it is an exothermic reaction.
(ii) The reaction of sodium metal is highly explosive because it is a strongly exothermic reaction.
(iii) When lead is treated with hydrochloric acid, bubbles of hydrogen gas are evolved.
Pb + 2HCl → PbCl₂ + H₂
items.ocr: 'The temperature of the reaction mixture gives rise' read as 'rises'.

items.stem:
State which of the following chemical reactions will take place or not, giving suitable reason for each:
(i) Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s)
(ii) Fe(s) + ZnSO₄(aq) → FeSO₄(aq) + Zn(s)
(iii) Zn(s) + FeSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Fe(s)
items.answer:
(i) Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s): this reaction will take place, as zinc is more reactive than copper and therefore can displace copper from its aqueous solution.
(ii) Fe(s) + ZnSO₄(aq) → FeSO₄(aq) + Zn(s): this reaction will not take place, since iron is less reactive than zinc and therefore will not be able to displace it.
(iii) Zn(s) + FeSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Fe(s): this reaction will take place, as zinc is more reactive than iron and therefore can displace iron from its aqueous solution.
items.ocr: The three equations were printed as one LaTeX array with the labels '(ii) (iii)' dumped afterwards; labels re-attached to their equations.

items.stem: Anhydrous copper sulphate (CuSO₄) was dissolved in one beaker and hydrated copper sulphate (CuSO₄·5H₂O) was dissolved in another beaker. What heat changes do you expect in these beakers and why?
items.answer: Dissolution of hydrated copper sulphate (CuSO₄·5H₂O) is an endothermic process, so the temperature of the solution falls in that beaker. Dissolution of anhydrous copper sulphate (CuSO₄) is an exothermic process — it hydrates as it dissolves — so the temperature of the solution rises in that beaker.
items.ocr: The printed answer key reverses the two cases, stating that anhydrous copper sulphate dissolves endothermically and hydrated copper sulphate exothermically. Dissolution of anhydrous CuSO₄ is in fact exothermic (it takes up water of hydration) and of the hydrate endothermic, so the answer has been recorded the correct way round and the conflict noted here.

items.stem: Tanya added magnesium into a test tube containing dil. HCl acid. She saw some gas coming out of it. She took a burning match stick near the mouth of the test tube and heard a popping sound while the match stick extinguished. Tanya concluded that the gas evolved is hydrogen and it is not combustible. Find the error in her conclusion and support your answer with reason.
items.answer: The conclusion that hydrogen gas is not combustible is wrong. Hydrogen gas is highly combustible and burns very fast, producing a large amount of heat — this rapid burning at the mouth of the test tube is what produces the pop sound and puts the match stick out. Tanya's identification of the gas as hydrogen is correct; only the statement about combustibility is in error.
items.ocr: 'hydrogen gas in highly combustible' read as 'is highly combustible'.

items.stem: Justify with the help of an example that a displacement reaction is also a redox reaction.
items.answer:
Consider the following displacement reaction:
Fe(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → FeSO₄(aq) + Cu(s)
iron + copper sulphate → iron(II) sulphate + copper (reddish brown)
In this reaction Fe is converted to Fe²⁺ by loss of electrons, hence Fe is oxidised. Cu²⁺ is converted to Cu by gain of electrons, hence Cu²⁺ is reduced. Thus the above reaction is a displacement reaction as well as a redox reaction.
items.ocr: 'redish brown' read as 'reddish brown'. The exam tag 'OD 2013' was printed in the middle of the answer's first line and has been moved to the section heading.

items.stem: Compound A when dissolved in water gives compound B and liberates heat. Compound A is used in white washing. Compound B reacts with CO₂ to form a white precipitate of compound C. Identify compounds A, B and C and also write the equations involved.
items.answer:
Quicklime (CaO) is used for whitewashing, so A is CaO.
CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ (slaked lime, calcium hydroxide) + Heat
So B is Ca(OH)₂.
Ca(OH)₂(aq) + CO₂ → CaCO₃ (calcium carbonate, white ppt.) + H₂O
So C is CaCO₃.
items.ocr: The 'Calcium Carbonate (White ppt.)' caption was printed twice; the duplicate has been removed. The second equation printed without its H₂O product; added.

items.stem: When CaO is added to water taken in a beaker, a rise in temperature is observed. However, when Ba(OH)₂ is mixed with NH₄Cl, a fall in temperature is observed. Why?
items.answer:
The reaction of CaO and water is an exothermic reaction, so a rise in temperature is observed.
The reaction of Ba(OH)₂ and NH₄Cl is an endothermic reaction, so a fall in temperature is observed.
Ba(OH)₂ + 2NH₄Cl + Heat → BaCl₂ + 2NH₄OH
barium hydroxide + ammonium chloride → barium chloride + ammonium hydroxide
items.ocr: Dropped 'i's restored in 'taken n a beaker', 'rise n temperature' and 'Cl s an endothermic reaction'. The ammonium hydroxide formula was split across a line break as '2NH_4' + 'OH'; rejoined as 2NH₄OH.

items.stem:
Give reasons for the following:
(i) Keeping food in air tight containers helps in preventing rancidity.
(ii) Moist air and acidic gases are not good for some metals.
(iii) Chips manufacturers usually flush bags of chips with nitrogen gas.
items.answer:
(i) An air tight container does not allow air (oxygen) to come into contact with the food, and this prevents oxidation of the food. Thus the food does not become rancid and its smell and taste remain the same.
(ii) Moist air causes corrosion (rusting) of iron, while acidic gases cause corrosion of copper and silver.
(iii) Nitrogen, being inert, prevents oxidation of the food (it displaces the oxygen inside the bag).
items.ocr: 'the food never become rancid' read as 'does not become rancid'.
